chapters.title: First Tablet
paragraphs:
The one who has witnessed Gilgamesh's story,
[the one] who knows all [that happened to him]

* * * together * * *

[The one] who has seen every kind of wisdom,
[who] knows the secrets and has looked on what is concealed,
brings news from further back [than the flood?];
he has travelled distant roads and grown weary * * *
[and has now written] all the rest on a memorial tablet

* * * the wall of Uruk-supuru.

[Lines ten and eleven are missing.]
He spoke a spell that will not leave [him]

* * * the god from long ago * * *.

* * * his cattle left him.

* * * he went down to the river,
pushed his boat into the river and covered it.

* * * overwhelmed by sorrow, he wept bitterly.

He returned (?) to Gan-gan-na, the city the enemy had utterly destroyed.
The female donkeys had trampled their foals;
the cows, crazed, turned on their calves.
As the livestock were frightened, so were the people.
The young women sighed and mourned like doves.
Erech's gods, the city of mighty walls,
took the shape of flies and buzzed through its streets.
Erech's guardian deities, the city of mighty walls,
turned into mice and hurried into their holes.
For three years the enemy kept Erech under siege;
the city's gates were barred and its bolts drawn.
Even Ishtar, the goddess, could not hold the enemy back.
Then Bel began to speak,
and addressed Ishtar, the queen:

chapters.title: Second Tablet
paragraphs:
Gilgamesh lets no son remain with his father,
no young woman with her warrior, no wife with her husband.
Their cries and grieving [are heard everywhere?].

"Gods of heaven, and you, Bel of Erech,
you who brought my son into being, [save us!?],
[there is] no rival [to Gilgamesh anywhere?].
Your people now come [to ask your help?].
Gilgamesh leaves no child with its father." By day and night [they made their plea]:

"He is Erech's ruler, the city of mighty walls.
He rules them and is
the strong, the towering, the cunning [* * *].
Gilgamesh leaves no daughter with [her mother?],
no young woman with a warrior, no wife with her husband."

[The heavenly gods] heard their appeal.
They too cried out to the goddess Aruru:
"Aruru, you who made him,
make him a rival (?) for the time when his heart is [* * *].
Let the two fight, and let Erech [watch them?]!"

Aruru heard and formed a man in her heart, in Anu's likeness.
She washed her hands, took a piece of clay and threw it to the ground.
That was how she made Eabani, the hero, a towering child, Ninib's possession (?).
Hair covered his whole body; long hair flowed from his head like a woman's.
His locks hung thickly, like the corn-god's.
Against?] the people's custom, he wore clothes like the god Ner.
He ate plants with the gazelles,
drank alongside the wild beasts,
and played among the water creatures.

Sa-a-a-du, the hunter of men,
kept watch beside the entrance to the well.
He stayed there on the first, second, and third day.
When Eabani came into view, the hunter's face grew troubled;
he looked over Eabani] and his animals, then went back home.
* * * he grieved, groaned and wailed;
his heart weighed on him, his face darkened,
and sadness settled in his mind.
His face took on the look of [the distant * * * (?)], and the sight stayed with him.

The hunter opened his mouth and said to [his father Ea or Shamash?]:
"Father, one hero going there [cannot be enough?].
In heaven there is * * *.
His strength is like the host of Anu.
He roams across [all] the mountains
and regularly [feeds] with the wild beasts.
His feet keep turning toward the mouth of the well.
I'm frightened of him; I don't dare to approach.
He filled in the pit I dug
and ruined the hunting nets I [had spread over it?].
He has driven the cattle and wild beasts from my hands
and won't let me hunt them."

[His father addressed the hunter and gave him this instruction]:
["Make your way] to the city of Erech, where Gilgamesh rules."

Gilgamesh told his hunter: "Take Uchat along, the woman who can coax Eabani away. When the animals reach the well, have her undress and stand exposed. Eabani will see her and come near; then the herd that keeps him company across the grasslands will turn and leave him."

The hunter and Uchat travelled without delay. After three days they arrived at the chosen ground and picked a place to stay. They hid beside the watering place while one day passed, then a second. It was where the cattle regularly drank and the water creatures played. Eabani came there from his mountain home, grazing with the gazelles, quenching his thirst alongside the herd, and taking pleasure among the living things in the water.

Uchat, the woman who lures people, caught sight of him * * *.

The hunter said to her, "There—our quarry! Uncover yourself and let him take pleasure in you. Do not shrink from him; welcome the force of his desire. Let him spot you and draw close. Slip out of your clothing so he can rest against you; meet his longing with a woman's love. Once he has pressed himself against you, the herd that grew up beside him on the plains will wander off and leave him."

Gilgamesh told his hunter: "Bring the woman Uchat along. She knows how to draw Eabani in. When the herds come to the well, she should strip and show herself. He will notice her and approach; then the animals that graze with him on the plain will desert him."

Uchat and the hunter set out on a direct route, reaching their destination after three days. They took up a resting place and waited. A day went by, then another, as they kept hidden at the water source. The cattle regularly came to drink there, along with the creatures living in the water. Eabani arrived from his highland home, grazing with gazelles, sharing the cattle's water, and finding joy among the water creatures.
Eabani listened and made up his mind.
Captivated by love, he turned back to the woman's feet
and looked up at the face of his temptress.
As she continued speaking, he listened closely.

The temptress said to Eabani:
"You are great, Eabani; you could be like a god.
Why lie down with the wild animals?
Come, I'll take you to walled Erech,
to the splendid home, the dwelling of Anu and Ishtar,
to Gilgamesh's palace; the hero is perfectly strong,
and towers over other men like a mountain bull."

Eabani answered the woman who had ensnared him:
"Come, Uchat, lead me there.
Take me to the splendid dwelling, the holy home of Anu and Ishtar,
to Gilgamesh's palace; he is the hero of perfect strength,
rising above other men like a mountain bull."

"Gilgamesh will see [you].
I glimpse [* * *] his face,
glowing with a hero's courage.
He is powerfully built, [magnificent?] in every part.
He is stronger than you.
He never stops [or tires?], by day or night.
Eabani, give up your [plan?].
Shamash loves Gilgamesh;
Anu, Bel and Ea whisper counsel in his ear.
Before you came down from the mountain,
Gilgamesh had already seen you in a dream at Erech."

chapters.title: Third Tablet
paragraphs:
* * * the gods let you enter
* * * was abandoned
* * * the partner * * *
* * * and he saw it by himself,
then unburdened his heart and spoke to his friend.
* * * I dreamed a dream in my sleep,
[The stars?] fell from the sky to the earth.
[Afraid?] I stood there.
* * * his face grew troubled
* * * his nails were like a lion's claws
* * * the dream?] gave me strength * * *.

"Come: he will give you a place to rest,
a richly made couch, finely appointed.
He will seat you in the place of honour at his left.
The rulers of the earth will bow to your feet.
Erech's people will call out to you * * *
and foreign nations will labour for you.
* * * all manner of things will be borne behind you
* * * he will make camp among them."

Eabani took in Shamash's words, the warrior's message,
* * * and the rage in his heart subsided.

chapters.title: Fourth Tablet
paragraphs:
We watched over you, great king [of the gods?].
Now watch over us in return.
To the lofty residence of the mighty queen, who knows all.

[In front of] Shamash he offered a smoke sacrifice,
poured out a drink offering,
and raised his hand before Shamash in prayer:
"Why have you disturbed Gilgamesh's heart?
Now you have instructed him;
he is travelling a long road to Humbaba.
He is about to enter a battle he has never known,
about to set out for a war he has never seen.
From his departure until he comes back,
until he reaches the splendid cedar forest,
until he has killed Humbaba the tyrant,
all the many dangers he meets will destroy him.
On the day when you * * *"

The country's forces came together;
the troops finished making ready,
and the warriors put on their armour.

The two companions then departed together.

Bel has made the cedar wood frightening to people so that it stays untouched.
Humbaba's roar was like a violent storm;
his mouth poured out curses, his breath (deadly?) like hot wind.
* * * hears a roar in the forest;
whoever goes down into his park.
Bel made the cedar forest a terror so it would remain untouched.
Pestilence (?) will strike anyone who enters it.

Before Shamash they dug a pit.
Gilgamesh went up to * * *
and tipped his offering meal into it, saying:
"Mountain, bring Eabani a dream!
Let him see visions in his sleep, Shamash."

"My friend, did you call me?"

The dream I had was dreadful (?);
the sky thundered, the earth shook;
day darkened and gloom rose;
lightning flashed, fire blazed,
full [of destruction] and stuffed with death.
Suddenly the light went dim, the fire went out,
* * * fell, became smoke * * *."

chapters.title: Fifth Tablet
paragraphs:
They stood there, and the forest rose high around them.
They stared in wonder at the tall cedars
and the gateway into the cedar forest,
where Humbaba used to stride with lofty steps.
Roads had been laid out and paths kept clear.
They saw Cedar Hill, home of the gods, Ernini's sacred place.
Before the hill stood a magnificent cedar,
beautiful, with a welcome shade that filled the heart with joy (?).
The corpse, food for the vultures.

chapters.title: Sixth Tablet
paragraphs:
He scrubbed his weapons and polished his armour.
He took off what he was wearing, put aside the dirty clothes, and dressed himself in clean garments.
He adorned himself and put on his crown (?).
Gilgamesh set the crown on his head and wore his headdress (?).

"Gilgamesh, join your life to mine and become my husband.
Let me have the full measure of your manly strength.
As your wife, I'll give you a chariot worked in gold and precious stones,
with gold wheels and shafts of sapphire (?).
You will harness great kudanu-lions to draw it.
The fragrance of cedar will meet you when you enter my home.
There you'll be seated in a high place,
while people press kisses to your feet.
Kings, lords and governors will bow to you.
Every fine thing from mountain and country will be brought as tribute.

* * * the sheep will give birth to twin lambs for you.

* * * they'll offer mules as tribute.

You'll ride in a splendid carriage,
drawn by a peerless team."

"Where is Tammuz, your husband, meant to live forever?
What became of the allallu bird * * *?
I'll tell you plainly what your love affairs lead to.
You made Tammuz, your young husband,
weep and mourn every year.
You loved the bright allallu bird,
but broke and crushed its wing.
Now it sits in the woods, crying, 'My wing!'
You loved the powerful lion too,
and dug a trap for him seven times over.
You loved the warhorse,
then drove it with bridle (?), spur and whip,
forcing it to run seven double-leagues without stopping.
When it grew tired and thirsty, you still drove it on,
bringing tears and grief to its mother Si-li-li." The mother Si-li-li wept in distress.

You also loved a shepherd * * *
who constantly burned incense for you
and slaughtered lambs every day to please you.
You struck him and changed him into a tiger,
so his own shepherd-boys drove him off
and his dogs tore him apart.

You loved your father's gardener too,
who kept bringing you delicacies
and dressing your table each day.
You looked at him and stirred his desire, saying:
"My farmer boy, let us enjoy your strength.
Extend your hand and take my virginity" (?).

The farmer answered you:
"Me! What are you asking of me?
Mother, you have not baked, so I will not eat.
The food I would have to eat is foul and bitter,
covered with cold and numbness."

When you heard him say this,
you struck him and made him a cripple (?),
forcing him onto a bed
where he could no longer get up.
Now you want me too; I'd meet the same fate as they did."

You had a shepherd among your lovers * * *.
He kept burning incense for you
and each day killed lambs to delight you.
You struck him, turned him into a tiger;
his own shepherds then chased him away,
and his own dogs ripped him apart.

Then there was your father's gardener, whom you loved.
He brought you treats again and again,
and arranged a fresh table for you every day.
You cast your eyes on him and inflamed his desire:
"My young farmer, let us share your strength.
Reach out your hand and take my virginity" (?).

But he replied:
"Why ask this of me?
Mother, you haven't baked, so I won't eat.
The meal I would get is sour and foul,
chilled and numbed over."

When you heard his refusal,
you beat him and transformed him into a cripple (?).
You made him lie on a bed
and left him unable to rise.
Now you want me as a lover; I would end up just like them."

They] pursued it, Eabani [attacked?] the Bull of Heaven,
* * * and seized it by its heavy tail.

Ishtar went to the wall of mighty Erech,
cried out sharply and cursed:
"Curse Gilgamesh, who has wounded me
and killed the Bull of Heaven!"

Eabani heard Ishtar's words,
tore off the bull's right haunch
and flung it in her face, saying:
"I'll defeat you this way;
I'll treat you just as I treated him;
I'll hang his heart (?) against your side."

The craftsmen marvelled at the bull's horns.
They were worth thirty minas of precious stones;
their thickness was half an inch (?)
and they held six measures of oil between them.
Gilgamesh dedicated them for anointing his god Lugal-tur-da.
He brought the horns and hung them in his lord's shrine.

They washed their hands in the Euphrates,
set out for the city by the road,
and rode through Erech's streets.

"Who among the heroes is glorious?
Who among men shines?"

"Gilgamesh is glorious among the heroes,
Gilgamesh shines among men!"

The craftsmen were amazed by the horns' size.
They were valued at thirty minas of precious stones,
and were half an inch (?) thick.
Together they held six measures of oil.
Gilgamesh set them aside to anoint his god Lugal-tur-da,
and hung them in the shrine of his lord.

They rinsed their hands in the Euphrates,
started down the road toward the city,
and rode through the lanes of Erech.

"Which hero stands out in glory?
Which man shines brightest?"

"Gilgamesh stands out among the heroes,
Gilgamesh is the brightest of men!"

chapters.title: Seventh Tablet
paragraphs: "Companion, tell me why the mighty gods have reached this decision."

chapters.title: Eighth Tablet
paragraphs:
No tree compares with you.
You stand six gar high and measure two gar across.

"My friend, I set out in good health. * * *
But what I dreamed has now come true."

Eabani lay on his couch for twelve days [from the first and second day?],
when he was [sick on his bed?];
then the third and fourth * * *.
On the fifth, sixth, seventh, eighth and following day,
Eabani remained [ill on his couch?].
The eleventh and twelfth day * * *
Eabani lay on his bed * * *.
Then he called out for Gilgamesh.

chapters.title: Ninth Tablet
paragraphs:
"I refuse to die the way Eabani did.
Grief has lodged inside me.
Terror at death has fallen over me,
and I am laid out on the earth.
I will set off now, and test Per-napishtim,
son of Kidin-Marduk, to see what strength he has."

"Night had fallen when I reached the mountain pass.
* * * I saw lions and was afraid.
* * * I raised my head to Sin and prayed.
My cry reached the [great?] god,
[he heard me] and rescued me."

In the night he saw?] a vision, a dream;
*lions * * *] were enjoying themselves.
He lifted the axe in his hand,
drew the sword from his belt,
and sprang among them like a spear.
He wounded them, killed them and drove [them?] apart.

As he reached Mount Mashu,
whose entrance the monsters guard each day,
whose back runs up to heaven's dam,
and whose breast descends to Aralu,
scorpion-men stood guard at its gate.
They spread dread; seeing them meant death.
Their terrible radiance could topple mountains.
From sunrise until sunset they guarded the sun.
When Gilgamesh saw them, his face darkened with fear.
Their wild appearance confused his mind.

One scorpion-man said to his wife:
"The one coming to us has a god's flesh for a body."
His wife answered:
"Two thirds of him resemble a god; only a third is human."

The scorpion-man replied:
"[One] of the gods has ordered it.
[He] has travelled far along distant roads
to come here to me.
The mountains] he crossed are steep."

For one mile he walks; dense night presses around him and no light comes.
For a second mile he travels; the dark stays thick and the way remains unlit.

chapters.title: Tenth Tablet
paragraphs:
Sabitu spotted him at a distance.
She spoke to herself,
considering what to do:
"Because this * * *
How will he succeed (?) in [what he seeks?]"

As he drew near, she shut [her sea-palace?].
She barred its gate, closing it again * * *.
Gilgamesh heard * * *
and raised his finger (?) * * *.
Then he called to Sabitu:
"Sabitu, why are you staring [at me?]
Why bar the gate against me?]
I'll break [your gate * * *."

Gilgamesh asked Sabitu for the route to Per-napishtim:
"Point me toward him; tell me the direction.
If a passage exists, I'll cross the sea;
if there isn't one, I'll run across the land."

Sabitu told Gilgamesh:
"No crossing has ever been made here;
from the beginning of time no one has passed over this sea.
Shamash alone makes the journey; who else could?
It is hard to traverse and the route is deadly.
The Waters of Death bar its entrance.
How could you cross this sea?
If you reached those waters, what would you do?
Yet Arad-Ea, the sailor who serves Per-napishtim, is nearby,
with the 'stone-men'; he cuts cedar in the woods.
Go and find him.
Try to make the crossing with him; if that cannot be done, turn back."

At this Gilgamesh lifted the axe in his arm,
drew the sword from his belt, plunged down toward [* * *],
and shot between them like a spear.

Arad-Ea said to Gilgamesh:
"Your hand has ruined the crossing.
You smashed the 'stone-men' * * *.
The 'stone-men' are broken, and * * * is gone.
Take the axe at your side, Gilgamesh.
Go into the woods and cut one hundred and twenty poles,
each five gar long."

Gilgamesh heard Arad-Ea's instruction.
He took his axe [and drew his sword].
He cut wood for a hundred and twenty poles, each five gar long,
coated them in pitch and carried them [to Arad-Ea].
Gilgamesh and Arad-Ea boarded the ship.
It bucked and rolled as they travelled.
A forty-five-day voyage was completed in three days,
and Arad-Ea brought them to the Waters of Death.

"Why are the ship's 'stone-men' smashed?
Who is this passenger, who is not my * * *?
Is he a man? Does he have a human side?
I look: what is this * * *? [Is it human?]
I look: what is this * * *? [A man?]
I look: what is this * * *? [A god?]
He looks just like me in every way."

"My beloved friend has turned to clay: Eabani, my companion.
I will not lie down as he did;
I will not sink to where he lies."

Gilgamesh said to Per-napishtim:
"I have come, and I will see Per-napishtim, whom people call 'the Distant'.
I will turn to him for help (?). I have travelled through all lands,
climbed steep mountains,
and crossed every sea."

chapters.title: Eleventh Tablet
paragraphs:
"I stare at you in wonder, Per-napishtim!
Your appearance is unchanged; you look like me.
Your nature has not altered; you look like me,
even though you have passed out of this life.
My heart still struggles with the things
that no longer burden you (?);
tell me how you came to live here
and gained everlasting life among the gods."

Per-napishtim replied to Gilgamesh:
"I will uncover the hidden account for you,
Gilgamesh; I will tell you what the gods kept secret.
Shurippak, the city familiar to you,
stands on the Euphrates' bank.
Its corruption led the gods there
to choose a flood for its fate—the great gods,
all of them: Anu, their father;
Bel, the warrior who counsels them;
Ninib, their chief;
and En-nu-gi, their champion.
Only Ea, whose wisdom has no bottom, disputed the plan.
He passed their secret to the walls of a reed dwelling:
'Reed walls, clay house, hear my words!
Reed walls, clay house, listen closely!
Man from Shurippak, child of Ubara-Tutu,
make yourself a home; build a vessel.
Give up your belongings; preserve your life!
Leave your goods behind; keep yourself alive.
Take into the vessel every kind of living seed.
When you build the vessel,
measure its proportions carefully:
let the span and length correspond,
then put it into the sea.'
I listened and answered my lord Ea:
'I will obey you, my lord;
I will heed this order and carry it through.
What should I say when the city asks,
and the people and elders demand an answer?'
Ea spoke to me, his servant:
'Tell them this:
"Bel despises me; I know it.
I cannot remain in your city any longer,
nor can I rest on Bel's land.
I will go down to the Deep and stay with Ea, my lord.
For a while he will send you abundant blessings:
fowl in plenty, fish beyond measure,
herds and a heavy harvest.
Shamash has named the hour:
at evening the dark powers will unleash a ruinous rain."'"

On the fifth day I laid out its shape.
Its sides stood ten gar high through the middle;
the deck also measured ten gar.
I built a roof over it and sealed it.
It had six storeys, seven floors all told;
I divided each level into nine compartments.
I cut openings inside for water.
I gathered a pole and all that was needed.
I coated the outside with three (or five) shar of pitch,
and the inside with three shar of asphalt to make it watertight.
The men carried three shar of oil in jars.
I kept one shar aside for offerings;
the boatman stored the other two.
I slaughtered oxen for the gods' temple (?)
and killed lambs (?) every day.
I poured out jugs of cider (?), oil and sweet wine,
large bowls of it, flowing like river water.
I held a feast for the gods like New Year's Day.
I offered oil to Shamash.
[* * *] the ship was finished.

The ship sank until water covered two thirds of its height.
I filled it with all I owned,
with all my silver,
with all my gold,
and with every kind of living creature.
I brought aboard all my family and kin,
field cattle, wild animals and honest people—everyone.

Shamash had set the time:
"When the dark lords send a destructive rain at dusk,
board the ship and shut its door."

The sign came true.
At dusk the dark lords sent the destructive rain.
I saw the storm drawing near
and feared to watch it.
I went into the ship and closed the door.
I entrusted its steering to Purur-bel, the boatman,
along with the great house and all it contained.

When dawn began,
a dark cloud climbed up from the horizon.
Adad, the storm-god, boomed inside it;
Nabu and Marduk, king of the gods, marched ahead.
Destroying powers crossed the mountains and the lowlands.
Great Dibbara tore the anchor cable (?) loose.
Ninib went forth, driving water over the riverbanks.
The Anunnaki raised their torches aloft,
and their fire lit the whole world.
Adad's gale climbed as high as heaven,
snuffing every light.
[       ] swamped the land like * * *.
In one day (?) it raged up above the mountains (??).
It attacked the people like an army charging.
No brother could tend to his brother;
people could no longer be recognised from the sky.
Even the gods panicked at the storm.
They withdrew into Anu's heaven,
where they squatted like frightened dogs,
pressed close along its enclosure.

Ishtar let out a labouring woman's scream,
and the Lady of the Gods broke into a loud lament:
"The world that once existed has crumbled back into clay.
I accepted this terrible plan in the gods' gathering.
Ah, that I should have agreed to it in their council!
I brought destruction upon my own people.
Where have all those I made gone?
They choke the sea like fish eggs."

The gods cried with her over the Anunnaki.
They drooped and wept where they sat,
their lips squeezed tight with fear.

For six days and nights
the wind blew; storm and tempest crushed the land.
As the seventh day approached, the tempest, storm and battle,
which they had fought like a great army, began to ease.
The sea settled; hurricane and gale died away.
I looked out across it and cried aloud,
but all humankind had turned to clay.
The whole surrounding plain had become riverbed.
I opened the air-hole, and daylight fell on my cheek.
Stunned, I sank back and sat crying,
tears streaming down my face.
I looked everywhere, and all I saw was sea.

Once twelve (days?) had passed, a strip of ground showed above the flood.
The vessel drifted until it reached Mount Nisir.
There it snagged and stayed fast.
For two days the mountain gripped the ship and let it go nowhere.
It held on during the third and the fourth day too.
The fifth and sixth days passed; still the vessel did not move.
As the seventh day approached,
I released a dove.
She flew in every direction,
found no place to settle and came back.
I sent out a swallow next.
She ranged around,
found no landing spot and returned as well.
Then I released a raven.
She saw the water level dropping as she flew.
She found food, departed and did not return. The ship remained pinned fast in the mountain, unable to slip from its grip.

I released everything to the four winds and made an offering.
I poured a libation on the mountain's peak.
I arranged seven pairs of censers,
filling them with calamus, cedar and fragrant incense.
The gods smelled the scent;
they breathed in the sweet fragrance
and swarmed around the sacrificer like flies.

"Gods, hear me! I swear by my necklace I won't forget this.
These days will remain in my memory; I will never erase them.
All the gods may come to this offering,
but Bel must stay away.
He acted recklessly when he brought on the flood
and delivered my people to ruin."

When Bel arrived and saw the ship,
he grew angry; fury against the Igigi filled his heart.
"Who escaped alive?
No one was meant to survive the great destruction."

Ninib answered the warrior Bel:
"Who but Ea could have planned it!
Doesn't Ea know every art?"

Ea replied to Bel:
"Wise god, mighty warrior,
why were you so rash as to unleash a flood!
Make the sinner pay for his sin,
and the wicked for his wickedness.
But spare them; do not destroy everyone!
Be merciful—let not everything be [confounded]!
Instead of a flood,
let lions reduce humankind;
instead of a flood,
let tigers reduce humankind;
instead of a flood,
let famine strike the land."

Bel finally reached a decision.
He boarded the ship, took my hand and led me ashore.
He brought my wife too, and had her kneel beside me.
Then he placed us face to face, stood between us and blessed us:
"Until now Per-napishtim was only a man.
From this day he and his wife will be raised among the gods.
Per-napishtim will live far from humankind, at the mouths of the rivers."
So they carried us far away to dwell at the rivers' mouths.

Per-napishtim now challenged him: "Which god can empower you and deliver the life you crave?" Then he ordered him: "Try to sleep!"
Gilgamesh lay as if paralysed for six days and seven nights;
a gale of slumber rolled over him.

Per-napishtim spoke to his wife:
"Look at this hero, whose heart is set on staying alive!
Sleep has swept over him like a storm."

His wife answered the man who lived far away:
"Wake Gilgamesh and have him eat the plant that restores health.
Let him recover, travel back along the route he came,
and pass through the great gate into his homeland."

Per-napishtim told his wife:
"His torment and pain have touched you.
Prepare a meal for him now and place it near his head."

As Gilgamesh slept aboard the vessel,
she cooked food for him.
First she prepared it; next she peeled and moistened it.
A fourth step cleaned the food (?);
she then added shiba, the mark of age,
and finally she cooked it.
At the seventh step, all at once,
the man changed after consuming the enchanted food.

Gilgamesh spoke to far-off Per-napishtim:
"I had collapsed and sleep had taken me.
Suddenly you worked a spell over me and helped me (?)"

Per-napishtim answered:
"* * * Gilgamesh, eat (?) your food.
* * * I will tell you:
first it was prepared, then peeled and dampened;
then your portion (?) was cleaned.
Shipa was added fifth;
sixth it was cooked;
seventh, I abruptly transformed you,
and you ate the enchanted meal."

Gilgamesh said to distant Per-napishtim:
"What am I to do now? Where should I go?
The death demon has taken my [companion?].
Death has claimed the couch beside me.
Where my * * * stands, death is there."

Per-napishtim said to the boatman Arad-Ea:
"Arad-Ea, let your boat carry you * * *.
Keep anyone who tries to board [the ship?] from coming aboard.
The man in front of you
is covered all over in sores;
the eruption has robbed his body of its beauty.
Take him to a place where he can be cleansed.
Let him wash until his sores turn white as snow.
Let the sea wash away the diseased skin he sheds.
His body will look healthy again.
Replace the head-wrap on his head
and dress his naked body.
Let the clothing last until he reaches his city
and completes his road.
It must remain fresh without losing [fibres?]."

Arad-Ea brought him to the cleansing place.
Gilgamesh washed until the sores turned white as snow.
He shed the damaged skin and the sea took it away.
His body looked healthy once more.
Arad-Ea put the head-wrap back on him
and covered him with clothes.
The garment was to last until the return to his city,
until he finished his journey;
[it stayed whole and new].

Then Gilgamesh and Arad-Ea sailed again,
the boat rocking as they went.

Per-napishtim's wife asked her distant husband:
"Gilgamesh has gone away, worked hard and pulled the oar.
What will you give him now to help him return home?"

Gilgamesh lifted the pole
and brought the boat closer to land.
Per-napishtim told him:
"You went away, laboured and pulled the oar.
What can I offer so you'll make it back home?
I will reveal something hidden,
and announce [the gods' decision] to you.
There is a plant like buckthorn,
whose thorn (?) stings like bramble.
When your hands can reach it * * *"

Gilgamesh understood the words and opened the * * *.
He fastened heavy stones [to his feet],
letting them draw him under the water [to reach the plant].
He seized the plant that could work magic.
He pulled free the weights [one fell away?],
then threw a second one toward the [first?].

He told Arad-Ea, the ferryman:
"This plant has marvellous power (or causes transformation?).
It grants people the wish they carry in their hearts.
I'll take it to well-fortified Erech, grow it there and cut it back.
It is called (?): 'The old will become young again!'
I'll eat it and regain my youthful vigour."

They kept a steady rhythm, eating after each twenty double-leagues
and resting every thirty.
Gilgamesh spotted a well filled with cool, refreshing water.
He climbed in and scooped some out.
A serpent-shaped demon darted up, and the plant slid from his grasp.
It surfaced [from the well?], seized the plant, and slipped away.
When he turned back, Gilgamesh cursed (?).
He sat and cried; tears ran along his cheeks.
He asked Arad-Ea:
"Why were my hands unsteady?
Why did the blood in my heart stop?
I brought no good fortune to myself;
the ground-lion (?) has gained it instead.
After only twenty double-leagues the plant was stolen,
right as I opened the well and lowered the bucket (?).
This portent tells me I must turn back
and leave the boat on the shore."

They resumed their routine, eating after each twenty double-leagues
and resting after each thirty,
until they reached strongly walled Erech.

Gilgamesh said to the ferryman:
"Go up and walk along Erech's wall.
Inspect its corner stone and examine the brickwork:
is the wall built of fired brick,
and is its foundation set in pitch (?)?
'Sevenfold is your name' (?)."

chapters.title: Twelfth Tablet
paragraphs:
"You will never again enter a temple [there?],
nor dress yourself in white [as before].
You lie fallen, like any mortal (?).
You will not smooth fragrant bull grease over your skin;
people won't come close for the scent of it.
Your bow no longer rests on the ground,
and the ones it struck now encircle you.
No staff remains in your hand;
the dead have taken you prisoner.
You won't bind sandals on your feet,
or send a battle shout across the earth.
You cannot kiss the woman you loved,
nor hit the woman you loathed.
You cannot kiss the son you cherished,
nor hit the son you despised.
The grief of the underworld has overtaken you,
and dark mother Nin-azu, dark as night,
whose luminous white body wears no cloth,
whose breast, like a case's lid, [remains * * *]." No sandals will strap your feet for you, and no shout of war will rise from your mouth on earth again.

"Father Bel, a fly's sting has knocked me down;
insects have beaten me to the ground.
Eabani [has gone down] to the shades.
Pestilence did not take him, and so on * * *.
Nergal's hidden, merciless demon [did not take him].
The battlefield did not kill him."

"Father Sin, an insect's bite has thrown me to the ground;
small vermin have brought me down.
Eabani [has gone down] among the shades.
It was not pestilence that took him, and so on.
Nergal's merciless hidden demon [did not take him]."

"Open the grave room and split the earth,
so Eabani's spirit may rise like a gust of wind
from below the ground."

When Nergal, the lord and hero, heard the appeal,
he smashed open the tomb chamber and rent the earth.
He raised Eabani's ghost from beneath the ground, like a wind.

"My dear friend, I beg you, describe
what the land you saw looks like!"

Eabani answered:
"I can't describe it, my friend; I can't.
If I showed you the country I have seen,
[Gilgamesh, surely you would?] sink down and weep."

[Gilgamesh answered?]: "Then I'll sit down and mourn!
[All that used to cheer you has become?] bitter and sad.
[Everything in the underworld?] is like an old robe, gnawed by worms.
The deeds [you did in this life?], the joys you once took,
[have disappeared?], all covered in dust."

One who lies on a soft couch and drinks clean water;
a warrior killed in battle—
"You and I have seen many such men—
his parents cradle his head,
and his wife kneels beside him.
Yes! Such a man's spirit can rest.
But one whose body lies unburied in the field—
You and I have seen such a person—
his ghost finds no peace in the earth, the land of the dead.
Someone whose spirit has no one to tend it—
You and I have seen that too—
must eat the bowl's scraps and dregs,
broken food thrown out into the street."
